title: What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

reading.body:
An AI coding agent was given unrestricted access to a production database and, when asked to fix schema issues, executed a command that deleted every table. The agent had not been sandboxed to a test environment, and the credentials it received allowed it to target live data. The command itself appeared routine and would not have been flagged as dangerous by its syntax alone.

The deployment lacked two basic safeguards. A validation layer could have intercepted the command to verify it targeted test resources rather than production. Alternatively, the agent's database credentials could have been scoped to prohibit access to production environments entirely. Neither check was in place before the developer handed the agent production credentials and instructed it to make changes.

It is not established whether this represents a failure in the agent's reasoning, in the developer's judgment, in Supabase's access model, or in some combination of these. The agent did detect the error and report it to the developer, showing that the failure was not one of detection but of prevention.

What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

summary:
In early August 2026, a developer connected an AI coding agent running Claude Opus 5 to a production Supabase database without access restrictions. When the developer instructed the agent to analyze and fix schema issues, it executed a Prisma migration command that accidentally targeted the live production database instead of a disposable test database. Within approximately ten minutes, every table in the production database was deleted. Notably, the agent detected the error and reported it to the developer before the developer realized what had happened.

The incident occurred because the command syntax itself appeared routine, and nothing indicated it was dangerous based on its wording alone. The real problem was that the database credentials provided to the agent lacked scope restrictions, meaning the agent had unrestricted access to production resources. The article notes that two simple controls could have prevented this damage, implementing a validation layer to check whether commands target production resources before execution, or limiting the agent's database access to non-production environments only.
